title: Things to Do in San Francisco: Three Stops for a Different View
description: Explore Pier 14, the Ferry Building waterfront and Pier 7 for three different views of San Francisco along the Embarcadero.
body:
For things to do in San Francisco that fit into a smaller outing, start along the Embarcadero. Pier 14, the Ferry Building’s bayside promenade and Pier 7 offer three ways to spend time with the waterfront, without requiring a cruise or a long climb through the hills.

The interest is in how the city meets the bay. Give each stop a little room and the walk can become more than a transfer between places to eat.

1. Start with a view from Pier 14

Pier 14 extends into the bay south of the Ferry Building near Mission Street. It is one of the public pedestrian piers identified in the Port of San Francisco’s waterfront plan.

Enjoy the relationship between the water and the buildings behind you from an open public position. You do not need to reach the far end to get something from the visit. It is a useful first stop for shifting your attention away from street traffic and toward the setting around the city.

Plan the stop: Check the gate and posted access notices. Weather and maintenance can change what is open. Use the pier only when accessible, keep away from edges and do not assume a clear day will reveal every distant landmark.

2. Give the Ferry Building’s waterfront its own moment

The Ferry Building sits at the foot of Market Street. Its official visit guide explains access by public transport and separates general building hours from individual business hours.

Before deciding where to browse or eat, spend a little time on the public bayside promenade. This is a working waterfront as well as a visitor destination. Watching its ordinary movement can be as interesting as finding the next item on a shopping list.

Plan the stop: Stay outside ferry boarding lanes and keep commuter routes clear. You do not need a ferry ticket for the public promenade. Marketplace purchases are optional, and the building and merchants have holiday closures to check separately.

3. Continue north to Pier 7

Pier 7 lies along the Embarcadero near Broadway. Its long form offers another way of looking back at the city and out over the water. San Francisco Travel includes the area in its waterfront parks and piers guide.

Let this be a slower final stop rather than an obligation to cover the whole pier. A place that looks simple on a map can become more engaging when you give the surroundings time to change. You can share the view with a friend without needing to agree on what is most interesting about it.

Plan the stop: Follow current public-access notices and leave space for other users, including people fishing. Bring a layer even if your day began in warm sunshine; an exposed waterfront can feel quite different.

Put the Embarcadero stops together

A straightforward order is Pier 14, the Ferry Building, then Pier 7. Allow around two to three hours if you want an unhurried outing with pauses. Meals and shopping can easily add time.

The suggested public viewing areas do not need attraction tickets. Food, transport and any ferry ride are separate. Use designated crossings when moving between the waterfront and city streets. If conditions close a pier, enjoy the open promenade rather than searching for another way through a barrier. Our San Francisco etiquette guide offers more visitor context.

Give the bay views a playful purpose
